text: Mavis Constance Tate (born Maybird Hogg; 17 August 1893 – 5 June 1947) was a British Conservative politician and campaigner for British women's rights. She was the daughter of Guy Weir Hogg (1861–1943), a diplomat who served as British consul for Portugal, Sweden, and Norway, a justice of the peace, and had business interests as managing director of SA Advertising Contractors in Cape Town, South Africa, and general manager of the Uganda Company; his wife, Constance, was daughter of Henry Joseph Marsden. Guy Hogg was grandson of Sir James Hogg, 1st Baronet, a politician and chairman of the East India Company. Mavis Tate’s brother, Kenneth, succeeded as the 6th baronet. As a Conservative, she was elected Member of Parliament (MP) for Willesden West in 1931, a seat typically held by Labour, and in 1935 moved to Frome, which she held with a majority of 994; Frome had been a Labour seat during the 1920s and was defeated by Labour in 1945. She was an early member of Archibald Ramsay's Right Club, founded in May 1939, but publicly protested Germany's mistreatment of Jews after Kristallnacht in 1938. After a nervous breakdown in 1940, she distanced herself from the far-right. In 1932, as MP for Willesden West, she opposed a clause in the National Health Insurance and Contributory Pension Bill that would penalise married women as 'malingerers and cheats' despite their full contributions. On the 1933 Employment Bill, she advocated for more training of the unemployed, stating it was better to train a smaller number thoroughly than to flood the market with undertrained workers. In 1934, during discussion of the Employment Assistance Act, she argued that destitute men and women should receive the same benefit amounts. She supported improvements in midwifery training due to 'terrible figures of maternal mortality' in 1935 and raised concerns about research into mental disorder and deficiency, particularly when sterilisation was proposed, questioning whether padded cells were a cure. She was a passionate advocate for equal pay, arguing that work should be paid according to its worth and that women had historically performed most of the country’s productive work before being excluded from working for gain; she criticized the government for systematically paying women less than men in the civil service and teaching profession, noting that this led to more women being employed and fewer men. She supported women's equal rights in nationality, stating married women should be in the same position as men, and presented a petition from 100 Commonwealth women's groups. By 1936, she was MP for Frome and supported the Marriage Bill for removing abuses in divorce law, highlighting the negative effects of illegitimacy on children whose parents were legally bound to partners in prison or asylums. She challenged the employment of 14-year-olds in factories, expressing concern over health deterioration and long hours, and reiterated her support for equal pay. She argued for better pensions for women, noting that women had typically earned less than men and thus saved less. She objected to clauses in the Marriage Bill implying that prolonged desertion did not end a marriage, quoting a clergyman that such a situation amounted to no Christian marriage. During World War II, she advocated for arming women to resist a feared German invasion in 1940 and cited the antisemitic writer Douglas Reed to support her call for the mass internment of refugees in 1940, stating that Jews were capable of acting as spies for Nazism. She chaired the Women's Power Committee in 1941 and the Equal Pay Campaign Committee in 1942, and was vocal on equal pay during the war. In two instances, she went against scientific and professional advice: in 1936, she challenged the government’s use of a living virus in smallpox vaccination; in 1939, she claimed the lymph vaccination method for soldiers, derived partly from rabbits, was likely to spread encephalitis and was extremely dangerous. In 1937, she objected to milk pasteurisation, citing constituents who disliked it, claiming the milk had negligible nutritive value and a nauseating taste; in 1939, she asserted that pasteurisation killed vitamins and hormones, calling it a 'pernicious practice'. A Royal Commission she requested on pasteurisation was not approved, and despite general support among MPs, she continued to argue that many people loathed pasteurised milk, despite evidence that 40% of pulmonary tuberculosis cases were linked to milk from unpasteurised sources. In April 1945, shortly before the end of WWII, Tate travelled with nine other MPs to visit the Buchenwald concentration camp in Germany to report on the atrocities; she narrated the newsreel for British Pathé News, stating "do believe me when I tell you that the reality was indescribably worse than these pictures." On 25 April, Earl Stanhope submitted the report to Prime Minister Winston Churchill, who presented it to Parliament on 27 April 1945. She married Captain Gerald Ewart Gott in 1915, divorced in 1925; in 1925 she married Henry Burton Tate, divorced in 1944. She adopted the first name "Mavis" in 1930 by deed poll. She suffered a nervous breakdown in 1940. Tate committed suicide by gassing herself and died at 6 Bloomfield Terrace, Westminster, on 5 June 1947, leaving an estate valued at £35,482,978. At her 1947 inquest, the Coroner for Westminster concluded she had committed suicide due to mental disturbance from ill-health. In a note to her brother, she wrote: "As I have no one dependent on me, it seems to be the wiser thing to end my life. An invalid is only a national liability. Today I cannot endure the extensive, constant pain in my head and I have had practically no sleep at all for week after week." Medical evidence indicated the effects of intense overwork, including severe kidney pain. Her brother, Col. Kenneth Hogg, said she was always trying to do too much. Her illness began after her visit to the Buchenwald concentration camp in 1945.
